pr_title: Pass content length into limited streams as Int64
pr_body:
Fixes: #75631

### Context
Problems from #75631 were caused by inconsistent/wrong casting Content-Length to int.

### Changes made
Passing content length as `long` wherever it was casted to int before.
Although it might be possible to verify it in `HttpClient.SendAsync` after we receive response from base, I feel like such validation shall be done in handlers anyway, and it actually is, so validation here would be mostly redundant.
I have simply pass proper uncasted content length value to receiving stream and let them throw in consistent fashion with former implemented validations.

### Result:
```
Content.ReadAsStringAsync
[   1 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.

Content.ReadAsByteArrayAsync
[   0 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.

GetAsync
[   1 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.

GetStringAsync
[   2 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.

GetByteArrayAsync
[   1 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.
```

Thanks for fixing this one.

Can we also fix the other inconsistency I mentioned:
> GetAsync (buffered SendAsync) will immediately validate the header length, but GetString/ByteArray helpers will read the content until the limit.

Where `LoadIntoBufferAsync` (hence also `GetAsync`) will check the `Content-Length` header upfront, but `GetString`/`GetByteArray` will try to read up to the limit first.

issue_context.title: Inconsistent large response content validation in HttpClient
comments:
Very nice writeup in description. I really do appreciate it.

I am able to fix `contentLength: int.MaxValue + 1L` cases however for:

```c#
using var client = new HttpClient(new MyHandler(contentLength: 101));
client.MaxResponseContentBufferSize = 100;
```

```
Content.ReadAsStringAsync
Reading content stream
[1497 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.

Content.ReadAsByteArrayAsync
Reading content stream
[1681 ms] Cannot write more bytes to the buffer than the configured maximum buffer size: 2147483647.
```

I am not sure we can afford to fix it. Currently we ignore `MaxResponseContentBufferSize` in  `response.Content.Read*` and as much as I think this behavior is wrong, as customer clearly state his intent to enforce `MaxResponseContentBufferSize`, such behavior is there for quite a while and it cloud break unknown number of customers, for example those whose response content is no longer as short as they expected it to be when they set `MaxResponseContentBufferSize` long time ago.

Please advice @karelz @MihaZupan @CarnaViire @ManickaP 

NOTE: During testing I have find out that when returned content stream is longer than declared in header, there is no error message. Fixing this, IMO, is also dangerous for back compatibility reasons.

That's right, changing `Content.ReadAs` helpers to enforce these limits would be a breaking change, even though I disagree with the current behavior.

I was suggesting we fix the `GetString`/`GetByteArray` helpers on `HttpClient`, both avoiding overflows and consistently checking the content length header up front.

review_comments: I have verified, by reading code, that `(new MemoryStream(0)).Capacity = c` vs `new MemoryStream(c)` have negligent affect on performance.
